American Franchise Act

This bill explicitly states that, for purposes of requirements under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), franchisors are only considered to be joint employers with their franchisees if they regularly exercise direct and immediate control over the terms and conditions of employment for a franchisee's employees (e.g., directly hiring or firing employees on a regular basis). (The NLRA provides for collective bargaining rights in the private sector. The FLSA provides for a minimum wage, overtime pay, and other standards for employment.)

Specifically, the bill provides statutory authority for a 2020 rule by the National Labor Relations Board, particularly in relation to franchisors and franchisees. Under this rule, an entity is considered a joint employer of a separate employer's employees under the NLRA only if the entity exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over one or more essential terms or conditions of employment. Essential terms or conditions of employment are defined to mean wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. (In 2026, the board reinstated the 2020 rule as the applicable standard.) 

The bill explicitly applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees and additionally specifies conduct that does and does not meet this standard (e.g., a franchisor setting a franchisee's operating hours does not sufficiently indicate direct and immediate control over the hours of work of a franchisee's employees). The bill also applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees under the FLSA.

Secure America Act

This act provides $70 billion in funding to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through FY2029 for immigration enforcement, border security, and related activities.

It is known as a reconciliation bill and includes legislation submitted by certain congressional committees pursuant to provisions in the FY2026 congressional budget resolution (S. Con. Res. 33) that directed the committees to submit legislation to the House or Senate Budget Committee that will increase the deficit. (Reconciliation bills are considered by Congress using expedited legislative procedures that prevent a filibuster and restrict amendments in the Senate.)

TITLE I--COMMITTEE ON HOMELAND SECURITY AND GOVERNMENTAL AFFAIRS

(Sec. 101) This section provides funding for CBP to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.

The funds provided by this section may not be used to recruit, hire, or train personnel for the duties of processing coordinators after October 31, 2028.

(Sec. 102) This section provides funding to ICE for (1) hiring, paying, training, and equipping Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents and support personnel; and (2) other necessary expenses for HSI’s mission support and operations and maintenance.

It also requires specified funds to be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts for certain HSI offices to (1) support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse, and (2) train such personnel and state and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse.

The funds provided by this section must be used for functions other than those related to HSI’s immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.

(Sec. 103) This section provides funding to CBP for border security, technology, and screening, including

  • procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment and associated civil works (e.g., artificial intelligence, machine learning, and other innovative technologies) and other mission support to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders;
  • upgrading and procurement of platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities;
  • upgrading and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders;
  • necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology, relating to the biometric entry and exit system under the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004;
  • enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders; and
  • necessary expenses for CBP's mission support and operations and maintenance for functions other than those related to its immigration enforcement and customs missions.

None of the funds provided by this section may be used for the procurement or deployment of surveillance towers along the southwest border and the northern border that have not been tested and accepted by CBP to deliver autonomous capabilities.

Under this section the term autonomous means a system designed to apply artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, or other algorithms to accurately detect, identify, classify, and track items of interest in real time such that the system can make operational adjustments without the active engagement of personnel or continuous human command or control.

(Sec. 104) This section provides additional funding to DHS for the purposes for which funding is provided in this title.

TITLE II--COMMITTEE ON THE JUDICIARY

(Sec. 201) This section provides funding to CBP for hiring, paying, training, and equipping CBP agents and the necessary support staff, and other necessary expenses for mission support and operations and maintenance, in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.

(Sec. 202) This section provides funding to ICE for immigration enforcement and related activities, including

  • hiring, paying, and training personnel;
  • transportation;
  • information technology;
  • facility and fleet maintenance and sustainment;
  • 287(g) agreements (i.e., agreements that allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions);
  • the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor;
  • operation and maintenance; and
  • operations by ICE to arrest certain unlawful aliens.

(Sec. 203) This section provides additional funding to DHS for (1) the purposes for which funding is provided in this title, (2) the assignment of certain DHS employees and state officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities, or (3) the participation of state and local agencies in certain homeland security efforts.

The following analysis is based on draft bill text that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.

Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act

This bill establishes an interagency task force to shut down criminal syndicates perpetuating mass online scams. This bill also explicitly authorizes sanctions against foreign individuals or entities operating or providing support to scam compounds. (Scam compounds target individuals for financial fraud and are concentrated in Southeast Asia.)  

The President must establish an interagency task force to shut down transnational criminal syndicates that use large scam centers and forced labor of trafficked persons to perpetuate mass online scams against Americans. The task force must submit to Congress and oversee implementation of a strategy to combat scam centers, dismantle the criminal elements involved with them, and hold corrupt officials accountable. The task force must periodically report to Congress, including a list of foreign persons sanctioned by the United States for their involvement with online financial scams from Southeast Asia against U.S. nationals.

The President is explicitly authorized to impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on (1) any foreign individual or entity that owns, controls, directs, or provides significant support to a significant scam compound operation or an enabling service; and (2) foreign government officials who knowingly enable or benefit from scam compound operations within their jurisdiction.

The Department of State is authorized to provide (1) trauma-informed care and other support services for trafficked persons within online scam centers, and (2) high-resolution satellite imagery to nongovernmental organizations and research institutions for the purposes of monitoring and documenting human rights abuses related to online scam centers in Southeast Asia.

Jordan McNair Student Athlete Heat Fatality Prevention Act

This bill requires certain institutions of higher education (IHEs) and secondary schools to develop and implement a venue-specific heat-related illnesses emergency action plan, including a plan for operating and using automatic external defibrillators and cold-water immersion equipment. The bill applies to (1) each IHE that participates in federal student aid programs and is a member of an athletic association or athletic conference, and (2) each secondary school that has a student athletics program.

Specifically, each plan must include a symptom identification structure and a coordination of care plan for student athletes exhibiting signs of heat-related illness that is posted in each locker room, athletic training facility, weight room, and outdoor sports complex and stadium.

Additionally, each plan must be

  • made available on the athletic program website or public website of the IHE or secondary school at the beginning of each academic year;
  • distributed to local emergency responders; and
  • distributed to, and practiced in person, by specific individuals (e.g., student athletes, coaches, and athletic trainers) before the start of practical training for each academic year.

The bill also requires an IHE and secondary school to submit an annual report that demonstrates compliance with this bill's requirements.

The Department of Education must inform secondary schools, local and state educational agencies, and IHEs about federal funds available to (1) assist with preventing heat-related illnesses, (2) develop heat-related illness prevention training, and (3) acquire equipment for treating heat-related illnesses for students and faculty.

Worldwide Animal Testing Compliance and Harmonization Act of 2026 or the WATCH Act

This bill requires foreign laboratories that receive federal funds for conducting animal research to undergo quarterly inspections to ensure compliance with U.S. animal welfare regulations.

The National Institutes of Health, in coordination with foreign authorities, must establish a process to inspect these laboratories on a quarterly basis to ensure compliance with U.S. animal welfare regulations, such as the use of animal care committees and evaluations of animal care and treatment. Laboratories that are found to be noncompliant, and that do not take appropriate corrective action, are subject to funding revocation.

Diversifying by Investing in Educators and Students to Improve Outcomes For Youth Act or the Diversify Act

This bill expands the Teacher Education Assistance for College and Higher Education (TEACH) grant program. The TEACH program awards grants to undergraduate and graduate students who commit to teaching in a high-need field and in an elementary or secondary school that serves low-income students.

First, the bill raises the maximum amount for TEACH grants.

Second, the bill allows TEACH grants to cover the full cost of attendance. Currently, these grants may be used only for tuition, fees, and on-campus housing.

The bill allows teaching in a high-need early childhood education program to count toward service requirements for the program.

Next, the bill eliminates the process for converting a TEACH grant to a loan if a recipient does not complete the requirements of the program. Further, the bill prohibits the Department of Education (ED) from instituting or creating a monetary penalty for failure or refusal to complete the service requirement.

In addition, the bill requires ED to send an electronic certificate to grant recipients who have completed their service requirement.

The bill also exempts the TEACH program from sequestration, which is a process of automatic, usually across-the-board spending reductions under which budgetary resources are permanently cancelled to enforce specific budget policy goals.
